notes: **กดมิเตอร์ด้วยนะครับ/ค่ะ is the most important sentence in this whole unit.** Literally "press the meter, please". In tourist areas some drivers offer a flat fare that can be two or three times the metered price. Saying this before you set off settles the matter without an argument — and if the driver refuses, just get out and find another taxi. That's normal, not an insult.
**ไปวัดโพธิ์ไหมครับ is said BEFORE you get in**, through the open window. Bangkok taxi drivers may turn down a destination, and asking first saves everyone time.
**ใช่ไหม châi mǎi means "right?"** and is used to confirm something you already suspect. Compare plain *ไหม mǎi*, which asks about something you don't know at all.
**ถึงแล้ว thǔeng láaeo = "we're here, we've arrived".** *ถึง* also means "to reach": *ไปถึงบ้าน* (to get home). It often appears together with *แล้ว*.

**ไม่ต้องทอน mâi tâwng thawn means "keep the change".** Tipping taxis isn't required in Thailand, but rounding the fare up is a common habit and always welcome. The word *ไม่ต้อง mâi tâwng* (no need) is covered fully in Unit 12.
**จอด jàwt means "to stop, park" for vehicles**, while *หยุด yùt* means "to stop" in general. To tell a driver to stop, use *จอด*: *จอดตรงนี้ครับ* (stop here).
**ตรง trong means both "straight" and "right at".** *ตรงไป* (straight ahead), *ตรงนี้* (right here), *ตรงไฟแดง* (right at the traffic light). One word, two jobs you'll often need.

**แน่ใจ nâae-jai means "sure, certain".** Notice the word *ใจ jai* (heart) at the end — Thai forms dozens of feeling words this way: *เข้าใจ khâo-jai* (to understand, literally "enter the heart"), *ดีใจ dii-jai* (glad), *เสียใจ sǐa-jai* (sad, sorry), *ใจดี jai-dii* (kind), *ใจร้อน jai-ráwn* (impatient, "hot-hearted"). When you see *ใจ*, you're looking at a word about feelings.

after: ⚠️ *เลย loei* has two very different jobs: as a verb it means **to go past** (*เลยไปหน่อย* = a little further past), and as a particle it means **"right away"** or **"at all"** (*ไม่ชอบเลย* = don't like it at all). The difference is always clear from its position.

after: **มอเตอร์ไซค์รับจ้าง** — the drivers wear orange vests and wait at the mouth of side streets. Literally "motorcycle for hire". For short distances in Bangkok it's almost always the fastest option, usually 20-40 baht.

⚠️ **A ตุ๊กตุ๊ก is almost always more expensive than a taxi** and has no meter. It's great fun to try once, but it's not an everyday way to travel. Bargain first, and agree on the price before you get in.

blocks.title: Two things that make asking for directions work better
items: **Show the name in writing, don't just say it.** Thai place names depend heavily on tone, and one wrong tone can make a name completely unrecognizable. Showing a phone screen with the name in Thai script solves this in a second.

⚠️ **Be wary of overly confident answers.** Thai culture is very reluctant to disappoint someone asking for help, so some people would rather point in any direction than say "I don't know". If the answer sounds hesitant, ask a second person — that's not rude, it's sensible.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern **โรง roong** in front of a word: it means "a large building for…". *โรงเรียน roong-rian* (school — building for studying), *โรงพยาบาล* (hospital — building for nursing), *โรงแรม* (hotel), *โรงหนัง roong-nǎng* (movie theater), *โรงงาน roong-ngaan* (factory). Just like *นัก-* and *ข้าง-*, one pattern unlocks many words at once.

blocks.title: If you're really lost
items: **ผม/ฉันหลงทางครับ/ค่ะ** *lǒng thaang* — I'm lost. This sentence almost always makes people stop and help.
**ช่วยหน่อยได้ไหมครับ/คะ** *chûai nàwy dâai mǎi* — could you help me for a moment?
**พาไปหน่อยได้ไหมครับ/คะ** *phaa pai nàwy dâai mǎi* — could you take me there? It's a big ask, but in Thailand it's granted surprisingly often.
